ORDER 


.....Petitioner 


This petition has been filed by the Petitioner against the Respondent Management under section 33-C (2) of 
the Industrial Dispute Act 1947 which is corresponding section 59 (2) under the Industrial Relation Code 2020 for the 
recovery of the amount Rs. 77,683.69ps with regard to legitimate dues of full and final payments including 


retrenchment allowances as per contract. 


2. Petitioner in his petition has averred that the 17 Respondent Visakhapatnam Steel Plant, got registered itself 
as Principal Employer under Central Legislative Enactment, "Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970." 
(Annexure 13) dated 14" August 2009, and (Annexure 14) dated 29" July 2011. The #/ Respondent "Midfield 


1040 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : MARCHY 7, 2026/PHALGUNA 16, 1947 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


Industries Limited," is licensed contractor under the Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970, and copy 
of the license is Annexure 17, dated 197 August 2009, confirming that the 27 Respondent is licensed to work as a 
contractor in the 17 Respondent industry establishment at Visakhapatnam. The 3™ Respondent "M/s Rishita 
Associates," is also licensed contractor by Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act 1970, and the license 
issued to the 37 Respondent is (Annexure 15) dated 6" November 2000. Further, Petitioner has averred that 
1“ Respondent acknowledged and accepted the 3" Respondent, Rishita Associates, as sub-contractor for the 
277 Respondent, Midfield Industries Limited, vide annexure 12, dated 157 September 2009. The 2™ Respondent and 
3" Respondent are licensed to work for the first Respondent, Visakhapatnam Steel Plant, at Visakhapatnam. Further, 
it is averred that the 1“ Respondent issued the work order to the 2™ Respondent vide work contract, 
dated 12" September 2009, under later of acceptance by the 2" Respondent, vide (Annexure 7) and the 
2™ Respondent accepted the work contract initially for a period of 24 months from 16" August 2009, and later it was 
extended for another 12 months, vide letter dated 177 October 2012, confirming the work contract extension up to 
15" August 2012, by (Annexure 8). Further, Petitioner averred that the 27 Respondent who engaged the Petitioner 
workmen as contact labour upon receiving the work contract (Annexure 7), later shifted all contact labour to the 37 
Respondent vide agreement between the 27 and 3 Respondents meant to execute work order of the 1" Respondent 
dated 12" September 2009. According to (Annexure 11) which is the agreement between the 2™ Respondent, 
"Midfield Industries Limited," and 3" Respondent, "Rishita Associates," dated 12.9.2009 for the work order dated 
16" August 2009, and same is binding agreement/settlement between the 2™ and 37 Respondents and is the 
foundation for the claim application for the recovery of the arrears as settled under (Annexure 11) settlement. Further, 
Petitioner has contended that Annexure-20 confirms that the 3™ Respondent Rishita Associates, received photo gate 
pass under (Annexure 11) in favour of the 86-contract labour including the Petitioner engaged by the 37 Respondent 
between the period of contract, i.e., 167 August 2009, to 15५ August 2012, for 36 months on behalf of the 
277 Respondent and (Annexure 20) is the photo identity gate pass cancellation order issued by 1“ Respondent for 86 
contract labour upon completion of the work contract. Further, it is averred that the Petitioner workmen are entitled 
to receive wages and terminal benefits upon the completion of the work contract, as contracted and settled under 
(annexure 11) between the second and 3rd Respondents for executing the work contract of the first Respondent and 
Petitioner is entitled to receive retrenchment allowances for contract labour at the rate of "actual working days/26 x 
month" 8 days. The Petitioner is unskilled and is entitled for the arrear of the amount due to words notice pay, service 
pay, and leave pay for 836 working days, amounting to Rs. 77,683.69ps_ Since both third Respondent as well as the 
2™ Respondent failed to pay the terminal benefits upon the completion of the work contract on 15" August 2012, 
Petitioner workman demanded the legal dues with interest from all Respondent collectively, but they did not pay. 
Further, it is submitted that after a lapse of nearly 15 months, 2" Respondent addressed a letter to the 1" Respondent 
(annexure 19) to make all the labour benefits payments directly to the workman such of that amount to be cleared 
against the work contract dated 12" September 2009, from pending amount due to the 2" Respondent’s account with 
the 17 Respondent. 17 Respondent acknowledged the letter, but no payment was made. Moreover, Petitioner union 
also addressed a letter (annexure 6) dated 247 March 2014, directly to 1st Respondent to release all the contract 
labour legal dues, and 11 Respondent acknowledged the same, but it was in vain. Further, it is averred that the 27 
Respondent, vide (annexure 5) dated 127 January 2015, addressed letter to the 17 Respondent requesting to settle all 
legal dues to the Petitioner contract labour and 1“ Respondent acknowledged the receipt of this letter but did not pay 
dues. Further, all the contract labour including Petitioner made representation through their union before the 
Regional Labour Commissioner Central Vishakhapatnam, vide (annexure 3) dated 19" August 2015, and (annexure 4) 
dated 20" July 2015. The concerned authority issued notices to all Respondents, but no relief was granted to the 
workman. Therefore, Petitioner has moved this petition under section 33C (2) of the ID Act for recovery of his 
legitimate dues from Respondent. Petitioner submitted that the 11 Respondent is legally bound to pay all the legal 
dues to the contract labour vide (Annexure 13) the undertaking given by the 1“ Respondent, and under section 21(4) 
of the Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act 1970 and Petitioner is also entitled to receive all the legitimate 
dues with interest at the rate of 18% per annum. 


3. Notice were issued to all Respondent. Respondent No.1 and Respondent No. 3 has filed their counter, but 
Respondent No. 2 did not file any counter despite service of notice. Therefore, case is proceeding ex-parte against 27 
Respondent. 


4. In response to notice Respondent No. 1 has filed counter and therein, he has contended that the petition filed 
by the Petitioner is not maintainable and is liable to be dismissed in limine. Further, it is contended that this 
Respondent awarded a contract to the 20 Respondent, Midfield Industry Limited, Hyderabad, a licensed contractor 
for the work of "strapping of mill products” vide work order No. VSP/WC/WRM/58485 -0/OT/2009- 10/8090000359 
dated 12" August 2009, for the period of 24 month, commencing from 1670 August 2009 to 15" August 2011. This 
contract was further extended for another period of 12 months with effect from 16" August 2011 to 157 August 2012. 
The 2™ Respondent contractor vide letter dated 127 August 2009, requested Respondent No. 1 to permit it to engage 
M/s Rishita Associates, Vishakhapatnam, sub/contractor, for supply of the labour for the subject contract work. 17 
Respondent considered request made by the 2" Respondent-contractor and, vide its letter dated 15" September 2009, 
approved the engagement of M/s Rishita Associates by the 27 Respondent as its sub-contractor. In the letter dated

10. Heard the argument of learned counsel for either parties. 


11. Perused the record. At the outset, Respondent counsel urged that present petition filed by the Petitioner for the 
recovery of full and final payment amounting to Rs.77,683.69ps. along with the interest for the work under contract is 
not maintainable under section 33-C(2) of ID Act 1947 as there is no amount due to the Petitioner from Respondent. 


Firstly, we have to examine provision contained under section 33 C (2) of the ID Act. Section 33 C (2) of ID Act 
provides :- 


"Where any workman is entitled to receive from the employer any money or any benefit which is capable of 
being computed in terms of money, and if any question arises as to the amount of money due or as to the 
amount at which such benefit should be computed, then the question may, subject to any rules that may be 
wait under this act, be decided by such labour court as may be specified in this behalf by the appropriate 
government within a period of not exceeding three month." 


12. Thus, in view of provision contained u/s 33-C (2) we proceed to examine the question whether the Petitioner is 
entitled to receive from employer any money or benefit which is capable of being computed in terms of money. 
Petitioner has filed affidavit therein he has disposed that in MP. No. 2/2017 Co-workman has disposed as WW in 
evidence and exhibited document W1 to W22. The evidence recorded in said petition may be treated as evidence of 
Petitioner in this case including cross examination of WW1. Since Petitioner has similar averment and evidence in 
both the petition. It is settled law that the rule of evidence Act do not apply strictly to the matter under I.D. Act. 
Therefore, evidence recorded in MPNo.2-2017 is taken on record and considered in this Petition in support of claim 
of Petitioner. In this context Petitioner has filed documents in evidence 


which has been exhibited by witness WW1.The perusal of these document reveals that the document Ex. W1 is the

Respondent No.1, Respondent No.2 and Respondent No.3 are jointly and severally liable to pay retrenchment 
allowances towards the full and final payment to the Petitioner as per contract. Although Respondent No.3 contended 
that it has paid all the money due to the Petitioner, but Respondent No.3 has not produced any document to establish 
that full and final payment as claimed by the Petitioner towards retrenchment allowances has been paid by 


[भाग Tavs 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : मार्च 7, 2026/फालगुन 16, 1947 1045 


277 Respondent or 37 Respondent. However, Respondent has filed photocopies of documents as proof of payment to 
the workman by R-2. The perusal of these photocopies goes to show that these are not proved by any cogent and 
relevant evidence of witness. Therefore, these photocopies in respect of payment are not admissible in evidence. 
Moreover, the genuineness of these document photocopies has been challenged by the Petitioner in his rejoinder, 
therefore, burden of proof to prove the factum of payment to the Petitioner lies on the Respondent No.1 which he 
failed to discharge. Thus, it is established that Petitioner is entitled to receive the amount towards benefits upon his 
retrenchment from service by R-3. Moreover, Respondent No.1 is the Principal Employer of Petitioner contract 
labour, therefore, Respondent No.1 is also liable to pay retrenchment allowances to Petitioner along with Respondent 
No.2 and Respondent No.3 jointly and severally. 


15, In this context, relevant decisions of the Hon’ble Supreme Court and High Court, are discussed as 
hereunder: - 


(a) In the case of Sail Growth Works versus Nilmani Lal and others, Writ Petition Number 386 of 2025, dated 10" 
March 2025, the Hon’ble High Court of Kolkata has held: 


19. Gratuity, payable under the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972, is a gratuitous payment required to be 
made by an employer to his employee at the time of termination of services of the employee or upon such 
employee’s death. 


Section 21 (4) of the Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970 (CLRA), mandates that a 
principal employer is responsible for the payment of 'wages' to a contract employee in the event of a contractor's 
failure to pay within the stipulated timelines or in the event of a contractor making a short payment. The principal 
employer then has the ability to recover the amount paid as 'wages', from the contractor. Section 2(h) of the CLRA 
defines the term 'wages' as all remuneration (whether by salary, allowances or otherwise) expressed in terms of 
money or capable of being so expressed, which would if the terms of employment, expressed or implied, were 
fulfilled, be payable to a person employed in respect of his employment or of work done in such employment and 
includes, among others, (६) any sum which by reason of the termination of employment of the person employed is 
payable under any law, contract or instrument which provides for the payment..."". However, it excludes (6) any 
gratuity payable on the termination of employees in cases other than those specified in (d)."" In Superintending 
Engineer, Mettur Thermal Power Station, Mettur vs. Appellate Page 11 Authority, Joint Commissioner of Labour, 
Coimbatore & Anr, 2012 LLR 1160, it has been held by the Madras High Court that gratuity payable under the 
Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 falls within this definition of 'wages'. The principal employer or the contractor may 
be liable to pay gratuity to contract employees, depending on the circumstances. Principal employer The principal 
employer is liable to pay gratuity to contract employees if the contractor fails to pay. The principal employer is 
liable to pay gratuity if the contractor makes a short payment. 


The principal employer is liable to pay gratuity if the contractor terminates the services of the contract 
employee. The principal employer is liable to pay gratuity if the contract employee works for multiple contractors. 
Contractor The contractor is liable to pay gratuity to contract employees if they have worked for at least five years 
and the contract is separate from the company. 


(b) In the case of Hindustan Steel Works Construction Limited versus Commissioner of Labour, Appeal Civil 
Number 11355 of 1996, dated 37 September 1996, the Hon’ble Court have held: - 


“The short question that arises for determination is whether the appellant who the principal employer is 
liable to pay to the contract workers any amount which constitutes the difference between the wages payable 
to the contract labour by the contractor and the wages paid by the appellant to its own employees doing 
similar work. The Division Bench seems to have relied upon Section 21(4) of the said Act for this purpose. 
Section 21(1), however, provides that the contractor shall be responsible for the payment of wages to each 
worker employed by his. Section 21(4) provides that if the contractor fails to make this payment or any part 
thereof, the principal employer is liable to make this payment and may recover the same from the contractor 
as set out in that sub-section. Looking to the definition of wages Under the said Act read with the definition 
of wages in the payment of Wages Act, which we have set out earlier, it is clear that Section 21 only deals 
with the payment of contractual wages by the contractor to each of his worker; The definition of wages 
would cover within its scope, inter alia, also those amounts which the contractor is liable to pay his workers 
under any award, settlement or order of court as well as other amounts falling within the definition of wages 
under the payment of Wages Act Subjection (2) provides for a representative of the principal employer 
supervising this payment. Clearly, therefore, the wages which are the subject-matter of Section 21 are 
specified sums which are payable in present by the contractor under the terms of his contract of employment 
with each worker as well as under any existing award, settlement or order of the court. -Section 21 does not 
deal with, nor does if cover the Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Rules, 1971. Hence Section 
21(4) will not apply to such obligations of the contractor which may be the subject-matter of dispute between 
the contractor and his workers at time of disbursement of wages and which do not fall within the definition 
of “wages” under the Act.” 


1046 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : MARCHY 7, 2026/PHALGUNA 16, 1947 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


(c) Further, Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case of M/s. Bombay Industries Chemical Industries Vs Deputy 
Labour Commissioner, Civil Appeal Number 813 of 2022, D.O.D dated 4" February 2022, the Hon’ble Supreme 
Court has held that the benefit sought to be enforced under Section 33C (2) of the ID Act is necessarily a pre-existing 
benefit or one flowing from a pre-existing right. The Hon’ble Court added that in the case of Kanku Ben, it is 
observed and held that whenever a workman is entitled to receive from his employer any money or any benefit which 
is capable of being computed in terms of money and which he is entitled to receive from his employer and is denied 
of such benefit can approach Labour Court Under section 33-C(2) of the ID Act. It is further observed that the benefit 
sought to be enforced Under Section 33C (2) of the ID Act is necessarily a preexisting benefit or one flowing from a 
preexisting right. The difference between a preexisting right or benefit on one hand and the right or benefit, which is 
considered just and fair on the other hand is vital. The former falls within jurisdiction of Labour Court exercising 
powers under Section 33C (2) of the ID Act, while the latter does not. 


(d) In the case of Jeet Lal Sharma versus Presiding Officer, 2001 VAD Delhi One, dated 157 March 2000, the 
Hon’ble High Court of Delhi have held:- 


“15. The point which is emphasised is that entitlement to receive money the pre-existing right can the 
based on (1) adjudication (2) settlement (3) service conditions. If the right to get a particular benefit is there, the 
application us. 13-C(2) would be maintainable and jurisdiction of Labour Court will not be barred merely because 
employer has denied the same 


16. What is the meaning of the expression "entitlement in receive". No doubt it is referable to pre-existing 
right. However where the workman claims a benefit flowing from a pre-existing right and approaches the Labour 
Courts 33-612) for computation of the right in term of money and the employer disputes the existences of the right, 
the Labour Court will have the jurisdiction to determine the question, whether the right exists and if the existence 
of right is established than in proceed in compute the benefit flowing therefrom in terms of money or on its 
decisions recovery proceedings start (New Taj Mahal Cafe Private Limited versus Labour Court reported in 1970 
(2) LLN 51 and East India Coal Company Limited (supra) In deciding the maintainability of the application u/s 
13-(12) what is in be looked at is the clans set up in the application and not what the other side contends in its 
reply. The fact that the employer by his plea rises some dispute, does not mean that Jurisdiction of Labour Court to 
deal with the question is taken away.” 


16. Thus, in view of forgone discussion and law laid down by Hon’ble Court as discussed above, Petition filed by the 
Petitioner under Section 33-C(2) of ID Act,1947 against the Respondents for recovery of retrenchment allowances as 
per Ex. W12 is acceptable. Undisputedly, Petitioner was engaged by Respondent No.3 M/s Rishitha Associates, and 
Respondent No.2 has engaged Respondent No. 3 as sub-contractor for Labour supply to work in the establishment of 
Respondent No.1 with prior approval vide document Ex. W8. Therefore, Respondent No.3 as such contractor for 
Labour supply for the work is responsible for payment of retrenchment allowances to the Petitioner. It has come on 
record Respondent No.3 has not paid the claimed amount to the Petitioner. Therefore, Respondent No. 3 and 
Respondent No.2 as main contractor is jointly and severally liable for payment of the claimed amount to the 
Petitioner. However, Respondent No.3 has contended that the Petitioner has not been retrenched by him and 
Petitioner is still continuing work with the Respondent No.1 under new contractor. Therefore, Petitioner is not entitled 
to recover retrenchment allowances from Respondent. Undisputedly, Petitioner was engaged by Respondent No.3 to 
work in the establishment of Respondent No.1 for the period from 16.08.2009 to 15.08.2012 as per Ex. W8. 
Respondent No.3 is no more employer of Petitioner after 15.08.2012 of the petitioner w.e.f 16-08-2012 and it makes 
no difference whether petitioner is still working with Respondent No.1 under some other contention. Thus, 
Respondent No.3 has retrenched services of Petitioner w.e.f 16.08.2012. 


The definition of retrenchment as provided under Section 2 (00) is extracted as here under: - 


2(00) “retrenchment “means the termination by the employer f the service of a workman for any reason 
whatsoever, otherwise than as punishment inflicted by way of disciplinary action but does not include--- 


(a) Voluntary retirement of the workman: or 


(b) Retirement of the workman on reaching the age of superannuation if the contract 
of employment between the employer and the workman concerned contains a 
stipulation in that behalf; or 


(bb) termination of the service of the workman as a result of the non-renewal of the 
contract of employment between the employer and the stipulation in that behalf 
contained therein; or” 


Although Petitioner might be working with Respondent No.1 even after 15.08.2012 but Respondent No.3 is no more 
employer of workman. Therefore, only conclusion can be drawn in such circumstances that Respondent No. 3 has 
terminated the service of Petitioner w.e.f 16.08.2012. Thus, Petitioner is entitled to receive retrenchment/allowance as 
per Ex. W12. Thus, the contention of R3 in this context is untenable. Therefore, the plea of Petitioner that Petitioner 
worker is working now under new contractor is untenable as the Respondent No. 3 is no more employer of the 
Petitioner after 15-08-2012 meaning thereby Petitioner has been terminated by Respondent No. 3 from service w.e.f 
16.08.2012 and is entitled to receive retrenchment allowances as per terns of the contract. 


[भाग avs 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : मार्च 7, 2026/फालगुन 16, 1947 1047 


17. | However, Respondent No. 1 has contended that terminal benefits claimed by the Petitioner do not form part of 
wages and as such the contractor as direct employer is responsible to make all other payments. In this context, the 
reference of definition of wages u/s 2 (1५७) Payment of Wages Act, 1936 is relevant. Therein it is provided that wages 
mean all remuneration (whether by way of salaries, allowances or otherwise) expressed in terms of money are capable 
of being so expressed which would if the terms of employment, expressed or employed were fulfilled be payable to 
person employed in respect of his employer or of work done in such employer and includes. 


(d) Any sum which by reason of termination of employment of the person employed is payable under any law 
contract or instrument which provides for the payment of such sum whether with nor without deduction but does not 
provide for the time within which the payment is to be made. 


Thus, in view of the above definition of wages the retrenchment allowances are very much covered under the 
definition of wages and the contention of the Respondent No.1 that retrenchment allowances are not included under 
the wages is untenable. According to Ex. W12 the term of payment/mode of payment has been agreed upon between 
Respondent No.2 the main contractor and Respondent No.3 sub-contractor, to be paid to the contract Labour i.e. 
Petitioner for doing the work at Respondent No.1 industry. The employment of Petitioner by Respondent No.3 of the 
Petitioner has been admitted by Respondent No. | & 2 and it is also admitted that retrenchment allowances of the 
Petitioner workman has not been paid by none of the Respondents. Therefore, as a Principal Employer Respondent 
No.1 is liable to pay retrenchment allowance to the Petitioner in view of the provision contained under Section 21 (4) 
of Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970 and he may recover the said amount of retrenchment 
allowances so paid to Petitioner from Respondent No. 2 and Respondent No. 3. Thus, the contention of Respondent 
No. 1 in this context is untenable. 


18. Therefore, in view of foregone discussion and law laid down by Hon’ble Court as discussed in preceding 
paragraph of this order, I come to irresistible conclusion that as per document Ex. W8 and W12 Petitioner had worked 
with the Respondent No. 1 as contract labour employed by Respondent No.3 as sub-contractor of Respondent No.2, 
during the period from 16-08-2009 to 15-08-2012 and Respondent No.3 the employer has terminated the services of 
Petitioner w.e.f 16-08-2012. Therefore, Petitioner is entitled for payment of retrenchment allowances as per 
document Ex. W12 which has been proved by the oral and documentary evidence of Petitioner and also admitted by 
Respondent No. 3 it is undisputed that none of the Respondents has paid such retrenchment allowance to the 
Petitioner. Therefore, as per provision contained under section 21 (4) of contract labour (Regulation and Abolition) 
Act, 1970 the Respondent No. 1 being principal employer is responsible for payment of retrenchment allowance to 
Petitioner, and he may recover said amount paid to Petitioner from Respondent No. | and 2 jointly and severally. 
Thus, the Petition filed by the Petitioner has merits and deserved to be allowed. 


ORDER 


The Petition filed by the Petitioner under section 33C(2) of ID Act 1947 corresponding section 59 (2) under 
the Industrial Relation Code is allowed. 


Respondent No. 1 Chairman & Managing Director, Rastriya Ispat Nigam Ltd, Visakhapatnam Steel Plant, 
Visakhapatnam is directed to pay the amount of Rs. 77,683.69ps. to the Petitioner within 30 days from the date of this 
order. Respondent No.1 is further directed to pay the interest @ 12% per annum on this amount from the date of due 
ie., 16-08-2012 up to the date of payment. 


It is further directed that Respondent No.1 is entitled to recover the said amount paid to Petitioner from 
Respondent No.2 the main contractor and Respondent No. 3 the sub-contractor jointly and severally. 


Ordered accordingly.

ORDER 


This petition has been filed by the Petitioner against the Respondent Management under section 33-C (2) of 
the Industrial Dispute Act 1947 which is corresponding section 59 (2) under the Industrial Relation Code 2020 for the 
recovery of the amount Rs. 76,011.08ps with regard to legitimate dues of full and final payments including 
retrenchment allowances as per contract. 


2. Petitioner in his petition has averred that the 17 Respondent Visakhapatnam Steel Plant, got registered itself 
as Principal Employer under Central Legislative Enactment, "Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970." 
(Annexure 13) dated 14" August 2009, and (Annexure 14) dated 29" July 2011. The one Respondent "Midfield 
Industries Limited," is licensed contractor under the Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970, and copy 
of the license is Annexure 17, dated 197 August 2009, confirming that the 27 Respondent is licensed to work as a 
contractor in the 17 Respondent industry establishment at Visakhapatnam. The 3™ Respondent "M/s Rishita 
Associates," is also licensed contractor by Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act 1970, and the license 
issued to the 37 Respondent is (Annexure 15) dated 67 November 2000. Further, Petitioner has averred that 1“ 
Respondent acknowledged and accepted the 37 Respondent, Rishita Associates, as sub-contractor for the 27 
Respondent, Midfield Industries Limited, vide annexure 12, dated 157 September 2009. The 2" Respondent and 3" 
Respondent are licensed to work for the first Respondent, Visakhapatnam Steel Plant, at Visakhapatnam. Further, it is 
averred that the 11 Respondent issued the work order to the 27 Respondent vide work contract, dated 127 September 
2009, under later of acceptance by the 2" Respondent, vide (Annexure 7) and the 2" Respondent accepted the work 
contract initially for a period of 24 months from 16" August 2009, and later it was extended for another 12 months, 
vide letter dated 177 October 2012, confirming the work contract extension up to 15"" August 2012, by (Annexure 
8). Further, Petitioner averred that the 21 Respondent who engaged the Petitioner workmen as contact labour upon 
receiving the work contract (Annexure 7), later shifted all contact labour to the 3™ Respondent vide agreement 
between the 27 and 311 Respondents meant to execute work order of the 1“ Respondent dated 12" September 2009. 
According to (Annexure 11) which is the agreement between the 2™ Respondent, "Midfield Industries Limited," and 
3" Respondent, "Rishita Associates," dated 12.9.2009 for the work order dated 167 August 2009, and same is binding 
agreement/settlement between the 2™ and 3" Respondents and is the foundation for the claim application for the 
recovery of the arrears as settled under (Annexure 11) settlement. Further, Petitioner has contended that Annexure-20 
confirms that the 37 Respondent Rishita Associates, received photo gate pass under (Annexure 11) in favour of the 


[भाग avs 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : मार्च 7, 2026/फालगुन 16, 1947 1051 


86-contract labour including the Petitioner engaged by the 3™ Respondent between the period of contract, i.e., 167 
August 2009, to 157 August 2012, for 36 months on behalf of the 27 Respondent and (Annexure 20) is the photo 
identity gate pass cancellation order issued by 17 Respondent for 86 contract labour upon completion of the work 
contract. Further, it is averred that the Petitioner workmen are entitled to receive wages and terminal benefits upon 
the completion of the work contract, as contracted and settled under (annexure 11) between the second and 3rd 
Respondents for executing the work contract of the first Respondent and Petitioner is entitled to receive retrenchment 
allowances for contract labour at the rate of "actual working days/26 x month" 8 days. The Petitioner is unskilled 
and is entitled for the arrear of the amount due to words notice pay, service pay, and leave pay for 818 working days, 
amounting to Rs. 76,011.08ps Since both third Respondent as well as the 2" Respondent failed to pay the terminal 
benefits upon the completion of the work contract on 15" August 2012, Petitioner workman demanded the legal dues 
with interest from all Respondent collectively, but they did not pay. Further, it is submitted that after a lapse of 
nearly 15 months, 27 Respondent addressed a letter to the 1“ Respondent (annexure 19) to make all the labour 
benefits payments directly to the workman such of that amount to be cleared against the work contract dated 12" 
September 2009, from pending amount due to the 27 Respondent’s account with the 1“ Respondent. 17 Respondent 
acknowledged the letter, but no payment was made. Moreover, Petitioner union also addressed a letter (annexure 6) 
dated 247 March 2014, directly to 1st Respondent to release all the contract labour legal dues, and 17 Respondent 
acknowledged the same, but it was in vain. Further, it is averred that the 976 Respondent, vide (annexure 5) dated 127 
January 2015, addressed letter to the 17 Respondent requesting to settle all legal dues to the Petitioner contract labour 
and 17 Respondent acknowledged the receipt of this letter but did not pay dues. Further, all the contract labour 
including Petitioner made representation through their union before the Regional Labour Commissioner Central 
Vishakhapatnam, vide (annexure 3) dated 197 August 2015, and (annexure 4) dated 20" July 2015. The concerned 
authority issued notices to all Respondents, but no relief was granted to the workman. Therefore, Petitioner has 
moved this petition under section 33C (2) of the ID Act for recovery of his legitimate dues from Respondent. 
Petitioner submitted that the 17 Respondent is legally bound to pay all the legal dues to the contract labour vide 
(Annexure 13) the undertaking given by the 1“ Respondent, and under section 21(4) of the Contract Labour 
(Regulation and Abolition) Act 1970 and Petitioner is also entitled to receive all the legitimate dues with interest at 
the rate of 18% per annum. 


3. Notice were issued to all Respondent. Respondent No.1 and Respondent No. 3 has filed their counter, but 
Respondent No. 2 did not file any counter despite service of notice. Therefore, case is proceeding ex-parte against 27 
Respondent. 


4. In response to notice Respondent No. 1 has filed counter and therein, he has contended that the petition filed 
by the Petitioner is not maintainable and is liable to be dismissed in limine. Further, it is contended that this 
Respondent awarded a contract to the 2" Respondent, Midfield Industry Limited, Hyderabad, a licensed contractor 
for the work of "strapping of mill products” vide work order No. VSP/WC/WRM/58485-0/OT/2009- 10/8090000359 
dated 12" August 2009, for the period of 24 month, commencing from 1670 August 2009 to 15" August 2011. This 
contract was further extended for another period of 12 months with effect from 16" August 2011 to 15" August 2012. 
The 2™ Respondent contractor vide letter dated 1270 August 2009, requested Respondent No. 1 to permit it to engage 
M/s Rishita Associates, Vishakhapatnam, sub/contractor, for supply of the labour for the subject contract work. 
1“ Respondent considered request made by the 2“ Respondent-contractor and, vide its letter dated 157 September 
2009, approved the engagement of M/s Rishita Associates by the 27 Respondent as its sub-contractor. In the letter 
dated 157 September 2009, 1“ Respondent clearly mentioned that clearance approved by it for engaging sub- 
contractor does not establish any contractual relationship between the sub-contractor Rishita Associates and 
Respondent No.1 Vishakhapatnam Steel Plant. It was clarified further that 2"’ Respondent contractor is not relieved 
from the Contractual obligations, responsibilities, and liabilities, etc. Further, Respondent contended that 86 contract 
labour are the contract labour of M/s Midfield Industries. The 2"' Respondent and as per the approval given by this 
Respondent, 2"! Respondent has subcontracted the work awarded to it to the third Respondent Rishita Associates 
vide Agreement Dt 16.8.2009 for execution of the work on behalf of the second Respondent/contractor and for 
purpose of execution of the contract work on behalf of the main contractor/second Respondent gate passes were also 
issued to the third Respondent/sub-contractor for the manpower engaged by it. As per the procedure, the gate passes 
should be cancelled immediately when once the contract comes to an end and full and final amounts will be settled by 
the contracting, agency, the second Respondent. Further, Respondent No. 2 should submit a proof to the Principal 
Employer/RINI, claiming reimbursement of the same. Respondent contended that third Respondent/sub- 
contractor/Rishita Associates had paid the wages to the contract labour for the total contract period after expiry of the 
contract period with the second Respondent, and entire contract labour including the Petitioner herein continued to 
work under a new contractor for the same work as the work of Strapping of Mill Products in WRM" is a continuous 
process. Further, it is submitted that second Respondent/contractor/Mid Field Industries submitted a request to RINL 
stating that it is entangled in income tax problems and requested to make payment in full and final due to its 
contractor labour, from out of the amounts due to it and pending with RINL. Accordingly, after obtaining due 
approvals and based on the amount due it was released by 1“ Respondent/RINL to 2™ Respondent/contractor paid an 
amount of Rs.28.58.522/- to the contract labour towards partial disbursement of terminal benefits. A copy of the 
payment particulars to contract labour in enclosed herewith and Petitioner has been paid Rs. 33,272/- out of the 
amount of Rs. 46,836/-.. The 2™ Respondent/contractor addressed a Letter di 19.02.2014 requesting the Principal 


1052 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : MARCHY 7, 2026/PHALGUNA 16, 1947 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


Employer/RINL to release the amount equivalent to full and final amount as a special case by making partial 
modifications to the agreement entered between it and 17 Respondent/RINL. Respondent made several reminders to 
the second Respondent/ contractor to submit its final bill till February 2013. Though the contract work was 
completed on 15.08.2012 but 27 Respondent/contractor did not respond to the same therefore, the 17 
Respondent/RINL processed the bill exparte. Respondent contended that as directions issued by the Income Tax 
Authorities to the Finance Department, this Respondent was supposed to deduct an amount of Rs 14,34,52,643/- as 
dues to be paid to the Income Tax Department from the pending bills of the second Respondent/contractor M/s 
Midfield Industries and accordingly, this Respondent deducted appropriate amount and paid to the Income Tax 
Department. Further, Respondent contended that the terminal benefit claimed by the Petitioner does not form part of 
wages and, as such the contractor as a direct employer is legally responsible to make all other payments if any to the 
Petitioner. Therefore, the petition is devoid of any merit and not legally maintainable, and it is liable to be dismissed. 


5. Respondent No. 2 did not turn up despite service of notice and nor filed any counter. Therefore, case is 
proceeding ex-parte against Respondent No. 2 vide order dated 20" September 2017 and being heard and decided 
exparte. 


6. Respondent No. 3 has filed his counter and therein it is contended that the averments made by the Petitioner 
in the petition are not true, valid, tenable, and petition filed by the Petitioner under section 33C(2) of the Industrial 
Disputes Act is not maintainable under law, as no amount is due and payable by this Respondent to the Petitioner. 
Further, Respondent No.3 contended that the first Respondent Rashtriya Ispat Nigam Limited/Visakhapatnam Steel 
Plant vide its Work Order dated 12th September 2009 awarded a contract for the work of "Scrapping of Mill Products 
in Wire Rod MHL to the second Respondent/Midfield Industries Limited, Hyderabad. Initially, contract period to 
work was for 24 months from 16.08.2009 to 15.08 2011 and later on it was extended for further period of 12 months 
commencing from 16.08.2011 to 15.08.2012. Further, it is contended that after obtaining approval from the first 
Respondent/ RINL, 2™ Respondent/Midfield Industries Limited of labour to carry out the contract work entrusted the 
work to Respondent No.3 on sub-contract basis i.e. for supply of contract labour between the first Respondent/RINL 
and second Respondent, work on commission basis and this Respondent has no other role in respect of Midfield 
Industries Ltd. While approving/permitting the second Respondent for giving the work to this Respondent on sub- 
contract basis, the first Respondent has clearly stated in their Letter dt. 15.09.2009 that the permission for engaging 
the sub-contractor does not establish or create between their Respondent and 21 Respondent/Midfield Industries 
Limited any contractual relationship or obligation between RINL and Respondent No. 2 is not relieved from the 
contractual obligations, liabilities and other responsibilities and he is alone responsible for any claim. This clearly 
establish that any dispute or claim by any third party, the first Respondent a Principal Employer and the Second 
Respondent as main Contractor are liable/responsible, and this Respondent is not liable for any claim made by the 
Petitioner. Further it is contended that prior to award of the Work contract labour including the Petitioner herein have 
worked under the previous contract by name M/s. Walzen Strips Private Limited and on completion of contract period 
of Mis Walzen Strips Private Limited on 15.08.2009 this work was awarded to the 27 Respondent/Contractor and 
thereafter to Respondent No.3 with prior approval of Respondent No.1 as mentioned in work order. This Respondent 
was engaged as sub-contractor and after completion of the period of the Work Order dt. 16.08.2009 on 15.08.2012 the 
obligations under sub-contract of the Respondent with the second Respondent came to end. Respondent No.3 
submits that Respondent contractors have not terminated or retrenched the services of workers at any point in respect 
of the said contract including the Petitioner herein and obligations on completion of the contract period does not arise. 
Respondent contractors have no obligation and Petitioner is not entitled to claim retrenchment compensation as his 
employment is still continuing under the subsequent contractors without any break in service. Further, it is contended 
that first Respondent RINL continued the second Respondent/contractor under a fresh work order with effect from 
16.08.2012 and contract labour including the Petitioner herein continued his services under the second 
Respondent/contractor. Hence in case of any claim by any contract labour much less the claim made by the Petitioner, 
it is for the first Respondent/RINL and the second Respondent/contractor to answer/respond the same and this 
Respondent is no way concerned with the claim of the contract labour. Further, Respondent submitted that on 
payment of amount made by the second Respondent/contractor, this Respondent paid the wages to all the contract 
labour including the Petitioner herein within time for the entire contract period of three years. There are no arrears of 
salary or any dues payable to the contract labour including the Petitioner herein. Further, it is contended that the first

10. Heard the argument of learned counsel for either parties. 


11. Perused the record. At the outset, Respondent counsel urged that present petition filed by the Petitioner for the 
recovery of full and final payment amounting to Rs.76,011.08ps. along with the interest for the work under contract is

1054 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : MARCHY 7, 2026/PHALGUNA 16, 1947 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


Firstly, we have to examine provision contained under section 33 C (2) of the ID Act. Section 33 C (2) of ID Act 
provides :- 


"Where any workman is entitled to receive from the employer any money or any benefit which is capable of 
being computed in terms of money, and if any question arises as to the amount of money due or as to the 
amount at which such benefit should be computed, then the question may, subject to any rules that may be 
wait under this act, be decided by such labour court as may be specified in this behalf by the appropriate 
government within a period of not exceeding three month." 


12. Thus, in view of provision contained u/s 33-C (2) we proceed to examine the question whether the Petitioner is 
entitled to receive from employer any money or benefit which is capable of being computed in terms of money. 
Petitioner has filed affidavit therein he has disposed that in MP. No. 2/2017 Co-workman has disposed as WWI in 
evidence and exhibited document W1 to W22. The evidence recorded in said petition may be treated as evidence of 
Petitioner in this case including cross examination of WW1. Since Petitioner has similar averment and evidence in 
both the petition. Therefore, evidence recorded in MPNo.2-2017 is taken on record and considered in this Petition in 
support of claim of Petitioner. In this context Petitioner has filed documents in evidence which has been exhibited by 
witness WW1.The perusal of these document reveals that the document Ex. W1 is the form of certificate issued by 
principal employer i.e., Deputy General Manager Visakhapatnam Steel Plant, Visakhapatnam to the effect that it has 
engaged M/s. Midfield industries Ltd Respondent No.2 for the work of strapping of mill product in WRM as 
contractor at Steel Plant, Visakhapatnam vide certificate dated 147 August 2009. Further, Document Ex. W8 is the 
letter dated 157 September 2009, issued by AGM works contract of Respondent No.1 addressed to M/s. Midfield 
Industries Limited.

of cogent and relevant evidence. Thus, on going oral and documentary evidence on record, it is established that the 
Petitioner workman is entitled to receive from the employer Respondent No.3 the amount of Rs.76,011.08ps. for the 
period of August,2009 to 2012 towards retrenchment allowances as per document Ex. W12. 


14. Now, question arises that who is liable to pay the said retrenchment allowances to the Petitioner as per 
contract. Admittedly, Petitioner workman was engaged by Respondent No.3 for the work of Respondent No.1. 
Respondent No.1 has admitted that the Petitioner had worked in the work of Strapping Mills Products WRM in its 
industry during the period from 16.8.2009 to 15.8.2012 as contract labour engaged by Respondent No.3. Since the 
Respondent No. 3 was sub-contractor for labour supply for the work order Ex. W8 of Respondent No.2, therefore, 
Respondent No.1, Respondent No.2 and Respondent No.3 are jointly and severally liable to pay retrenchment 
allowances towards the full and final payment to the Petitioner as per contract. Although Respondent No.3 contended 
that it has paid all the money due to the Petitioner, but Respondent No.3 has not produced any document to establish 
that full and final payment as claimed by the Petitioner towards retrenchment allowances has been paid by 
277 Respondent or 37 Respondent. However, Respondent has filed photocopies of documents as proof of payment to 
the workman by R-2. The perusal of these photocopies goes to show that these are not proved by any cogent and 
relevant evidence of witness. Therefore, these photocopies in respect of payment are not admissible in evidence. 
Moreover, the genuineness of these document photocopies has been challenged by the Petitioner in his rejoinder, 
therefore, burden of proof to prove the factum of payment to the Petitioner lies on the Respondent No.1 which he 
failed to discharge. Thus, it is established that Petitioner is entitled to receive the amount towards benefits upon his 
retrenchment from service by R-3. Moreover, Respondent No.1 is the Principal Employer of Petitioner contract 
labour, therefore, Respondent No.1 is also liable to pay retrenchment allowances to Petitioner along with Respondent 
No.2 and Respondent No.3 jointly and severally. 


15. In this context, relevant decisions of the Hon’ble Supreme Court and High Court, are discussed as 
hereunder: - 


(a) In the case of Sail Growth Works versus Nilmani Lal and others, Writ Petition Number 386 of 2025, dated 
10" March 2025, the Hon’ble High Court of Kolkata has held: 


19. Gratuity, payable under the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972, is a gratuitous payment required to be 
made by an employer to his employee at the time of termination of services of the employee or upon such 
employee’s death. 


Section 21 (4) of the Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970 (CLRA), mandates that a 
principal employer is responsible for the payment of 'wages' to a contract employee in the event of a contractor's 
failure to pay within the stipulated timelines or in the event of a contractor making a short payment. The principal 


1056 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : MARCHY 7, 2026/PHALGUNA 16, 1947 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


employer then has the ability to recover the amount paid as ‘wages’, from the contractor. Section 2(h) of the CLRA 
defines the term 'wages' as all remuneration (whether by salary, allowances or otherwise) expressed in terms of 
money or capable of being so expressed, which would if the terms of employment, expressed or implied, were 
fulfilled, be payable to a person employed in respect of his employment or of work done in such employment and 
includes, among others, ''(d) any sum which by reason of the termination of employment of the person employed is 
payable under any law, contract or instrument which provides for the payment..."". However, it excludes (6) any 
gratuity payable on the termination of employees in cases other than those specified in (d)."" In Superintending 
Engineer, Mettur Thermal Power Station, Mettur vs. Appellate Page 11 Authority, Joint Commissioner of Labour, 
Coimbatore & Anr, 2012 LLR 1160, it has been held by the Madras High Court that gratuity payable under the 
Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 falls within this definition of 'wages'. The principal employer or the contractor may 
be liable to pay gratuity to contract employees, depending on the circumstances. Principal employer The principal 
employer is liable to pay gratuity to contract employees if the contractor fails to pay. The principal employer is 
liable to pay gratuity if the contractor makes a short payment. 


The principal employer is liable to pay gratuity if the contractor terminates the services of the contract 
employee. The principal employer is liable to pay gratuity if the contract employee works for multiple contractors. 
Contractor The contractor is liable to pay gratuity to contract employees if they have worked for at least five years 
and the contract is separate from the company. 


(b) In the case of Hindustan Steel Works Construction Limited versus Commissioner of Labour, Appeal Civil 
Number 11355 of 1996, dated 377 September 1996, the Hon’ble Court have held: - 


“The short question that arises for determination is whether the appellant who the principal employer is 
liable to pay to the contract workers any amount which constitutes the difference between the wages payable 
to the contract labour by the contractor and the wages paid by the appellant to its own employees doing 
similar work. The Division Bench seems to have relied upon Section 21(4) of the said Act for this purpose. 
Section 21(1), however, provides that the contractor shall be responsible for the payment of wages to each 
worker employed by his. Section 21(4) provides that if the contractor fails to make this payment or any part 
thereof, the principal employer is liable to make this payment and may recover the same from the contractor 
as set out in that sub-section. Looking to the definition of wages Under the said Act read with the definition 
of wages in the payment of Wages Act, which we have set out earlier, it is clear that Section 21 only deals 
with the payment of contractual wages by the contractor to each of his worker; The definition of wages 
would cover within its scope, inter alia, also those amounts which the contractor is liable to pay his workers 
under any award, settlement or order of court as well as other amounts falling within the definition of wages 
under the payment of Wages Act Subjection (2) provides for a representative of the principal employer 
supervising this payment. Clearly, therefore, the wages which are the subject-matter of Section 21 are 
specified sums which are payable in present by the contractor under the terms of his contract of employment 
with each worker as well as under any existing award, settlement or order of the court. -Section 21 does not 
deal with, nor does if cover the Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Rules, 1971. Hence Section 
21(4) will not apply to such obligations of the contractor which may be the subject-matter of dispute between 
the contractor and his workers at time of disbursement of wages and which do not fall within the definition 
of “wages” under the Act.” 


(c) Further, Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case of M/s. Bombay Industries Chemical Industries Vs Deputy 
Labour Commissioner, Civil Appeal Number 813 of 2022, D.O.D dated 4" February 2022, the Hon’ble Supreme 
Court has held that the benefit sought to be enforced under Section 33C (2) of the ID Act is necessarily a pre-existing 
benefit or one flowing from a pre-existing right. The Hon’ble Court added that in the case of Kanku Ben, it is 
observed and held that whenever a workman is entitled to receive from his employer any money or any benefit which 
is capable of being computed in terms of money and which he is entitled to receive from his employer and is denied 
of such benefit can approach Labour Court Under section 33-C(2) of the ID Act. It is further observed that the benefit 
sought to be enforced Under Section 33C (2) of the ID Act is necessarily a preexisting benefit or one flowing from a 
preexisting right. The difference between a preexisting right or benefit on one hand and the right or benefit, which is 
considered just and fair on the other hand is vital. The former falls within jurisdiction of Labour Court exercising 
powers under Section 33C (2) of the ID Act, while the latter does not. 


(d) In the case of Jeet Lal Sharma versus Presiding Officer, 2001 VAD Delhi One, dated 157 March 2000, the 
Hon’ble High Court of Delhi have held:- 


“15. The point which is emphasised is that entitlement to receive money the pre-existing right can the 
based on (1) adjudication (2) settlement (3) service conditions. If the right to get a particular benefit is there, the 
application us. 13-C(2) would be maintainable and jurisdiction of Labour Court will not be barred merely because 
employer has denied the same 


16. What is the meaning of the expression "entitlement in receive". No doubt it is referable to pre-existing 
right. However where the workman claims a benefit flowing from a pre-existing right and approaches the Labour 
Courts 33-612) for computation of the right in term of money and the employer disputes the existences of the right, 


[भाग 1---खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : मार्च 7, 2026/फालगुन 16, 1947 1057 


the Labour Court will have the jurisdiction to determine the question, whether the right exists and if the existence 
of right is established than in proceed in compute the benefit flowing therefrom in terms of money or on its 
decisions recovery proceedings start (New Taj Mahal Cafe Private Limited versus Labour Court reported in 1970 
(2) LLN 51 and East India Coal Company Limited (supra) In deciding the maintainability of the application 
u/s 13-(12) what is in be looked at is the clans set up in the application and not what the other side contends in its 
reply. The fact that the employer by his plea rises some dispute, does not mean that Jurisdiction of Labour Court to 
deal with the question is taken away.” 


16. Thus, in view of forgone discussion and law laid down by Hon’ble Court as discussed above, Petition filed by the 
Petitioner under Section 33-C(2) of ID Act,1947 against the Respondents for recovery of retrenchment allowances as 
per Ex. W12 is acceptable. Undisputedly, Petitioner was engaged by Respondent No.3 M/s Rishitha Associates, and 
Respondent No.2 has engaged Respondent No. 3 as sub-contractor for Labour supply to work in the establishment of 
Respondent No.1 with prior approval vide document Ex. W8. Therefore, Respondent No.3 as such contractor for 
Labour supply for the work is responsible for payment of retrenchment allowances to the Petitioner. It has come on 
record Respondent No.3 has not paid the claimed amount to the Petitioner. Therefore, Respondent No. 3 and 
Respondent No.2 as main contractor is jointly and severally liable for payment of the claimed amount to the 
Petitioner. However, Respondent No.3 has contended that the Petitioner has not been retrenched by him and 
Petitioner is still continuing work with the Respondent No.1 under new contractor. Therefore, Petitioner is not entitled 
to recover retrenchment allowances from Respondent. Undisputedly, Petitioner was engaged by Respondent No.3 to 
work in the establishment of Respondent No.1 for the period from 16.08.2009 to 15.08.2012 as per Ex. W8. 
Respondent No.3 is no more employer of Petitioner after 15.08.2012 of the petitioner w.e.f 16-08-2012 and it makes 
no difference whether petitioner is still working with Respondent No.1 under some other contention. Thus, 
Respondent No.3 has retrenched services of Petitioner w.e.f 16.08.2012. 


The definition of retrenchment as provided under Section 2 (00) is extracted as here under: - 


“2(00) “retrenchment “means the termination by the employer f the service of a workman for any reason 
whatsoever, otherwise than as punishment inflicted by way of disciplinary action but does not include--- 


(a) Voluntary retirement of the workman: or 


(b) Retirement of the workman on reaching the age of superannuation if the contract 
of employment between the employer and the workman concerned contains a 
stipulation in that behalf; or 


(bb) termination of the service of the workman as a result of the non-renewal of the 
contract of employment between the employer and the stipulation in that behalf 
contained therein; or” 


Although Petitioner might be working with Respondent No.1 even after 15.08.2012 but Respondent No.3 is no more 
employer of workman. Therefore, only conclusion can be drawn in such circumstances that Respondent No. 3 has 
terminated the service of Petitioner w.e.f 16.08.2012. Thus, Petitioner is entitled to receive retrenchment/allowance as 
per Ex. W12. Thus, the contention of R3 in this context is untenable. Therefore, the plea of Petitioner that Petitioner 
worker is working now under new contractor is untenable as the Respondent No. 3 is no more employer of the 
Petitioner after 15-08-2012 meaning thereby Petitioner has been terminated by Respondent No. 3 from service w.e.f 
16.08.2012 and is entitled to receive retrenchment allowances as per terns of the contract. 


17. | However, Respondent No. 1 has contended that terminal benefits claimed by the Petitioner do not form part of 
wages and as such the contractor as direct employer is responsible to make all other payments. In this context, the 
reference of definition of wages u/s 2 (IV) Payment of Wages Act, 1936 is relevant. Therein it is provided that wages 
mean all remuneration (whether by way of salaries, allowances or otherwise) expressed in terms of money are capable 
of being so expressed which would if the terms of employment, expressed or employed were fulfilled be payable to 
person employed in respect of his employer or of work done in such employer and includes. 


(d) Any sum which by reason of termination of employment of the person employed is payable under any law 
contract or instrument which provides for the payment of such sum whether with nor without deduction but does not 
provide for the time within which the payment is to be made. 


Thus, in view of the above definition of wages the retrenchment allowances are very much covered under the 
definition of wages and the contention of the Respondent No.1 that retrenchment allowances are not included under 
the wages is untenable. According to Ex. W12 the term of payment/mode of payment has been agreed upon between 
Respondent No.2 the main contractor and Respondent No.3 sub-contractor, to be paid to the contract Labour i.e. 
Petitioner for doing the work at Respondent No.1! industry. The employment of Petitioner by Respondent No.3 of the 
Petitioner has been admitted by Respondent No. | & 2 and it is also admitted that retrenchment allowances of the 
Petitioner workman has not been paid by none of the Respondents. Therefore, as a Principal Employer Respondent 
No.1 is liable to pay retrenchment allowance to the Petitioner in view of the provision contained under Section 21 (4) 
of Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970 and he may recover the said amount of retrenchment 
allowances so paid to Petitioner from Respondent No. 2 and Respondent No. 3. Thus, the contention of Respondent 


1058 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : MARCHY 7, 2026/PHALGUNA 16, 1947 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 
No. 1 in this context is untenable. 


18. Therefore, in view of foregone discussion and law laid down by Hon’ble Court as discussed in preceding 
paragraph of this order, I come to irresistible conclusion that as per document Ex. W8 and W12 Petitioner had worked 
with the Respondent No. | as contract labour employed by Respondent No.3 as sub-contractor of Respondent No.2, 
during the period from 16-08-2009 to 15-08-2012 and Respondent No.3 the employer has terminated the services of 
Petitioner w.e.f 16-08-2012. Therefore, Petitioner is entitled for payment of retrenchment allowances as per 
document Ex. W12 which has been proved by the oral and documentary evidence of Petitioner and also admitted by 
Respondent No. 3 it is undisputed that none of the Respondents has paid such retrenchment allowance to the 
Petitioner. Therefore, as per provision contained under section 21 (4) of contract labour (Regulation and Abolition) 
Act, 1970 the Respondent No. 1 being principal employer is responsible for payment of retrenchment allowance to 
Petitioner, and he may recover said amount paid to Petitioner from Respondent No. 1 and 2 jointly and severally. 
Thus, the Petition filed by the Petitioner has merits and deserved to be allowed. 


ORDER 


The Petition filed by the Petitioner under section 33C(2) of ID Act 1947 corresponding section 59 (2) under 
the Industrial Relation Code is allowed. 


Respondent No. 1 Chairman & Managing Director, Rastriya Ispat Nigam Ltd, Visakhapatnam Steel Plant, 
Visakhapatnam is directed to pay the amount of Rs. 76,011.08ps. to the Petitioner within 30 days from the date of this 
order. Respondent No.1 is further directed to pay the interest @ 12% per annum on this amount from the date of due 
ie., 16-08-2012 up to the date of payment. 


It is further directed that Respondent No.1 is entitled to recover the said amount paid to Petitioner from 
Respondent No.2 the main contractor and Respondent No. 3 the sub-contractor jointly and severally. 


Ordered accordingly.

-------- Applicant/Workman 
Versus 
1. Admn. Commander Station Head Quarter (Civil Defence), Chandi Mandir Cantt. Panchkula, Haryana. 
2. M/s AA Foundation for Safety, Head Office 5919, DLF City, Face-4, Gurugaon-122022. 
----Respondents 
Present:- Sh. Jang Bahadur, AR for workman. 
Sh. Satinder Singh, AR for respondent no.1. 
Respondent no.2 already ex parte. 
Award : 02.02.2026 


1. Workman has filed the present claim petition under Section 2A of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 
(hereinafter called the Act) against his termination w.e.f. 27.10.2018 claiming reinstatement into service 
along with continuity of service and full back wages. 


2. It is maintained by the workman in the claim petition that that he was appointed as sweeper/safai 
karamchari on 01.11.2017 by respondent 10.1 at minimum wages prescribed by the Central Government. 
But the said minimum wages were never paid to him. Management has unlawfully deducted 12% EPF 
share, 1.75% ESI and Rs.300/- as TDS from his salary despite of the fact that his total wages comes under 
the ambit of tax free limit. He was working under respondent no.1 directly, but respondent no.1 in order to 
avoid its liability always shows his employment in record under different contractors, which tantamount 
to unfair labour practice. 


3. It is further maintained that workman including 200 other safai karamcharis of respondent 10.1 raised the 
demand for non-deduction of TDS from the wages paid by respondent 10.1. However, their demand was 
not accepted. Other workers working under respondent 10.1 formed union and subsequently his services 
were dispensed with w.e.f. 27.10.2018. It is also maintained that respondent 10.1 retained juniors in 
service and also made fresh appointments after termination of his services and no compensation was paid 
under Section 25F of the Act. Thus, there is violation of Section 25F, 25G and 25H of the Act. Hence this 
petition. 


[भाग 1---खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : मार्च 7, 2026/फालगुन 16, 1947 1061 


4. 
5. 


6. 


Notice of the petition was given to respondents. 


Respondent 10.1 filed reply to the claim petition maintaining therein that the workman has not come to 
the Court with clean hands as he was appointed as sweeper by respondent no.2 (contractor) at minimum 
wage rate as prescribed by the Central Government. As per Government Policy dated 18.03.2011 (Ex.R- 
1), Non-Cantonment Military Stations have been authorized to outsource conservancy safaiwala. The 
answering respondent entered into contract with various private agencies for outsourcing of sweepers 
(safai karamcharis). In July 2018, the answering respondent entered into contract with M/s AA 
Foundation for safety and M/s Sunrise Facilitator Pvt. Ltd. through e-tendering for outsourcing of safai 
karamcharis to provide conservancy services in Chandi Mandir Military Station for the financial year 
2018-19. Respondent no.2 submits bill for payment for the days the safai karamcharis performed their 
duties and answering respondent is only responsible to forward these bills to PCDA Western Command 
Chandigarh to release payment directly to the contractor’s account. Salary is paid to the workman by the 
contractor. Compliance of PF, ESI Rules etc. is carried out by the contractor as per contract agreement. 
Answering respondent has no responsibility of disbursement of wages and deduction of EPF and ESI etc. 
The workman and other safai karamcharis formed union in the headquarter, which is not permitted and 
also carried out demonstration inside the premises of Station Headquarter on 27.10.2018 and failed to 
perform his duties. Thereafter, answering respondent asked respondent no.2 to ask the workers to perform 
their duties. Answering respondent has no role or responsibility for termination services of the workman. 
There is no relationship of employer and employee between the answering respondent and the workman. 
In view of Army Headquarter Letter, the civilian employees of the answering respondent cannot organize 
themselves into trade unions as station headquarter is an administrative office of the Government of India. 
In spite of that, workman along with other safai karamcharis formed union unauthorizedly and indulge in 
unlawful activities. It is maintained that workman is the employee of contractor and therefore, termination 
is the prerogative of the contractor. It is prayed that the claim be dismissed. 


It is pertinent to mention here that respondent no.2 was proceeded ex parte on 07.05.2024. 


Evidence of workman:- 


de 


In order to prove his case, workman examined himself as WWI and tendered into evidence his affidavit 
WWI/A and has been cross examined by the AR for respondent 10.1. AR for workman closed the 
evidence on 22.07.2024.

8. Respondent 10.1 examined Colonel K P Singh S/o Late Colonel P. P. Singh, OIC, Civic Cell, Station 
Head Quarter, Chandi Mandir Panchkula as MW1, who tendered into evidence his affidavit Ex. MW1/A 
along with documents Ex.R1 to Ex.R4. AR for respondent 10.1 closed the evidence on 29.01.2026.

Submissions of workman:- 


9.While arguing the case, AR for workman contended that in this case, workman was appointed by respondent 


10.1 under a camouflage agreement with respondent no.2. The workman was appointed directly by 
respondent 10.1 on 01.11.2017 as sweeper and his services were dispensed with on 27.10.2018 without 
any reason in violation of Section 25F, 25G and 25H of the Act as no compensation was paid to the 
workman and junior to him were retained in service and fresh appointment were made after termination of 
the workman. So far as the agreements between the respondent 10.1 & 2 are concerned, they are totally 
not tenable and is unfair labour practice. The work performed by the workman is of perennial in nature. 
The contractor was not having any license. The contractor has left after three months. No domestic 
inquiry was held before terminating the service of the workman, which is mandatory under the Act. 


Submissions of respondent no.1:- 
10. On the other hand, AR for respondent no.1 contended that the workman was engaged by respondent no.2 


(contractor) as per agreement executed between respondent 10.1 & 2 on outsource basis and there is no 
relationship of employer and employee between respondent 10.1 and the workman. Wages were paid by 
the respondent 10.2 to the workman and there was no role of respondent 10.1 in appointing or terminating 


1062 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : MARCHY 7, 2026/PHALGUNA 16, 1947 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


the services of the workman. Workman is employee of respondent no.2. If there is any violation of 
provision of the Act, then it is done by respondent no.2. As per Ex.R3, all dues were paid by the 
contractor with regard to EPF and ESI etc. The workman and other safai karamcharis formed union in the 
Headquarter, which is not permitted as per Ex.R4. Respondent 10.1 being the Government Agency, 
workman is trying to take benefit of his appointment by respondent no.2 and has filed a false claim after 
concealing material facts and claim of the workman is not maintainable. 


11. Ihave given due consideration to the arguments advanced by AR for both the parties. 


Findings:- 

12. The first contention regarding the applicant is that whether applicant comes within the definition of 
workman as is defined in Section 2(s) of the Act. I may mention that applicant was appointed as sweeper 
as per his claim petition and affidavit submitted before the Tribunal. In plain words the applicant was 
performing his duties as labourer/unskilled worker. He was not in supervisory or administrative post 
requiring him to perform only administrative duties. While interpreting Section 2(s) Hon’ble Supreme 


Court in the case of Devinder Singh Vs. Municipal Council, Sanaur, AIR 2011 Supreme Court 2532, 


has observed as follows:- 


“The source of employment, the quantum of recruitment, the terms & conditions of employment contract of 
service, the quantum of wages/ pay and mode of payment are not at all relevant for deciding whether or not a 
person is a workman within the meaning of Section 2(s) of the Act. The definition of workman also does not 
make any distinction between full time and part time employee or a person appointed on contract basis. 
There is nothing in the plain language of Section 2(s) from which it can be inferred that only person 
employed on regular basis or a person employed for doing whole time job is a workman and the one 
employed on temporary, part time or contract basis on fixed wages or as a casual employee or for doing duty 
for fixed hours is not a workman.” 


13. Thus Hon’ble Supreme Court has clarified that the definition of workman also does not make any 
distinction between full time or part time employee or a person appointed on contract basis. There is 
nothing in plain language of Section 2(s) from which it can be infer that only person employed on regular 
basis or a person employed for doing whole time job is a workman and the one employed on temporary, 
part time or contract basis on fixed wages or as a casual employee or for doing duty for fixed hours is not 
a workman. In view of the ratio of law enunciated in the above ruling, in my considered opinion the 
applicant herein admittedly falls within the definition of ‘workman’ under Section 2(s) of the Act. 


14. The Hon’ble Supreme Court after analyzing the catena of cases has laid down in Balwant Raj Saluja Vs. 
Air India Limited in Civil Appeal _No.10266 dated 25.08.2014, two well recognized tests to find out 


whether the labours are the contract employees of the principal employer are:- 
1) Whether the principal employer pays the salary instead of contractor and 
2) Whether the principal employer controls and supervise the work of the employees? 


15. The facts regarding the payment of salary by the management or contractor has not been stated in the 
claim petition of the workman. In fact, claim petition is totally silent regarding the payment of wages, 
salary, letter of appointment by respondent 10.1 or by contractor or anything likewise. Thus, this basic 
feature for holding the relationship of employer and employee i.e. between respondent 10.1 and workman 
totally lacking not in the pleading but also in the evidence submitted by the workman. However, MW1 
Colonel K P Singh in his cross examination has stated that it is responsibility of the contractor to pay 
monthly wages to the conservancy staff provided by him. Respondent no.1 has nothing to do with the 
minimum wages, DC rate to the conservancy staff. Contractor is responsible to give notice to the 
conservancy staff provided by him. Respondent 10.1 has no roll in terminating the services of the 
workman. Thus, it was the respondent no.2 who was required to ensure the payment of wages to the 
workers engaged by him from time to time. 


16. It is also added here that respondent 10.1 has also placed on record documents Ex.R-1 to Ex.R-4. Ex.R-2 
is the contract agreement between respondent 10.1 & 2. Thus, from the adduced evidence, it emerges that 
workman was paid salary by the contractor and he was being controlled and supervised by the contractor. 
Thus, there does not exist any relationship of employee and employer between the workman and 
respondent 10.1. However, there exists relation of employee and employer between the workman and 
respondent 10.2. 


17. It is also added here that as per definition of contractor as given in the Section 2(c) of the Contract Labour 
(Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970 (hereinafter called as Contract Act), respondent no.2 was supplying 
contract labour to the respondent 10.1. Thus, respondent no.2 would fall under the definition of 
contractor. Section 2(c) of the Contract Act is reproduced as under: 


[भाग पए--ख एण्ड 3(1i)] भारत का राजपत्र : मार्च 7, 2026/फालगुन 16, 1947 1063 


“Contractor”, in relation to an establishment, means a person who undertakes to produce a given result for the 
establishment, other than a mere supply of goods or articles of manufacture to such establishment, through 
contract labour or who supplies contract labour for any work of the establishment and includes a sub- 
contractor; 


18. 


19. 


20. 


21. 


22. 


23. 


24. 


25. 


26. 


The Hon’ble Apex Court in the case of Banglore Water Supply & Sewerage Board Vs. A. Rajappa 
1978(36) FLR 266 dealt at length with the ambit and scope of expression “industry” as defined in Section 


2(j) of the Act, and has laid down triple test for determining whether a particular establishment is industry 
or not. The triple test is where (a) systematic activity (b) organized by cooperation between employer and 
employee (the direct and substantial element is commercial (c) for the production or distribution of goods 
and services to calculated to satisfy human wants and wishes prima facie is an “Industry” in that 
enterprise. The workman was doing work i.e. systematic activity for respondent 10.1 at the asking of 
respondent no.2 and there was cooperation between the workman and respondent no.2, which involve 
substantial commercial element for rendering service to satisfy human wants. Thus, respondent no.2 
would be termed as industry. 
Workman in his deposition has clearly stated that there was non-compliance of Section 25F, 25G and 25H 
of the Act. He also stated that he was appointed on 01.11.2017 and he was paid minimum wages 
prescribed by Central Government and was working with respondent 10.1. He was not given any 
compensation before terminating his services on 27.10.2018. In his cross examination, he has further 
stated that his salary used to be credited in his bank account. But he has not placed on record any bank 
account, in which his salary was credited in order to enable this Court to see who was making payment to 
the workman. However, there is no denial that the workman was paid salary by respondent no.2 
(contractor). However, from the agreement dated 05.07.2018 (Ex.R-2) placed on file by respondent no.1, 
it emerges that safai karamcharis were provided by respondent no.2 (contractor) to work with respondent 
10.1. Thus, workman was employee of respondent 10.2 and not of respondent 10.1 as has been discussed 
above. There does not exist any relationship of employee and employer between the workman and 
respondent 10.1. However, there exists relation of employee and employer between the workman and 
respondent 10.2. 
Admittedly, there is non-compliance of Section 25F of the Act by respondent no.2. However, as regards 
violation of other provisions i.e. Section 25G and 25H of the Act, there is no evidence lead by the 
workman. Hence, workman is entitled for compensation from respondent 10.2. 
It is also added here that there is no iota of evidence that any unfair labour practice used by respondent 
10.1 by entering into contract with contractors for supply of safai karamcharis and agreement executed 
between respondent no.1 and 2 cannot be said to be any unfair labour practice. So far as contentions of 
AR for workman that the work performed by the workman is of perennial in nature and no domestic 
inquiry was held before terminating the services of workman are concerned, in this regard, it is pointed 
out that workman was entitled only for compensation under Section 25F of the Act by respondent no.2 
(contractor) and no domestic inquiry was required to be conducted. Merely because work is of perennial 
in nature does not mean that any right has accrued in favour of the workman to get employment with 
respondent 10.1, which is a department of Civil Defence run by Government of India and for that regular 
recruitment procedure is provided. Workman cannot seek backdoor entry into service. Moreover, 
workman is not employee of respondent 10.1 being employee of respondent 10.2 (contractor). 
In view of above discussion, it is held that since respondent no.2 (contractor) is currently not working 
with respondent 10.1, so keeping in view the tenure of service rendered by the workman and salary given 
to him during the period of his stay with the contractor and non-compliance of Section 25F of the Act, this 
Tribunal is of the considered opinion that workman is entitled for compensation. 
Keeping in view the fact and circumstances of the present case, the following scheme of compensation is 
deemed fit by this Tribunal: 
1. Workman who worked for less than 2 years with contractor shall be entitled for Rs.20,000/-. 
ii. | Workman who worked for more than 2 years but less than 5 years with contractor shall be entitled 
Rs.30,000/-. 


ili. Workman who worked for more than 5 years with contractors shall be entitled for Rs.50,000/-. 


Present workman employed on 01.11.2017 and was terminated on 27.10.2018 (less than 2 years), so he is 
entitled for Rs.20,000/-. 

Respondent no.2 is directed to pay the workman Rs.20,000/- within one month from the date of the 
notification of the award failing which the respondent no.2 shall further pay interest @6% per annum 
from the date of award till the date of making payment. It is also added here that in case respondent no.1 
requires safai karamcharis, then workman may be engaged through any contractor on sympathetic ground. 
Let copy of this award be sent to Central Government for publication as required under Section 17 of the 
Act. 


KAMAL KANT, Prtesiding Officer

4. Notice of the petition was given to respondents. 


[भाग 1---खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : मार्च 7, 2026/फालगुन 16, 1947 1065 


5. Respondent no.1 filed reply to the claim petition maintaining therein that the workman has not come to the

prescribed by the Central Government. As per Government Policy dated 18.03.2011 (Ex.R-1), Non-Cantonment
